title: Core2 loop busy-polls with delay(100) and never sleeps — battery drained in hours
problem: The Core2 loop calls M5.update() then delay(LOOP_DELAY_MS=100) forever. delay() on ESP32 is a busy/idle spin that does NOT enter light sleep, so the CPU runs continuously at 80 MHz, the BLE radio stays in full-power connectable advertising, and (see separate finding) the LCD backlight is never dimmed. There is no esp_pm_configure / light_sleep_enable, no automatic modem sleep tuning, no deep sleep. The CoreInk sibling does all of this (initPower(), light_sleep_enable=true, event-driven ulTaskNotifyTake) and claims ~1 mA / 14 days; the Core2 here will sit at tens of mA just from CPU+backlight+radio. On the Core2's ~390-500 mAh battery this is roughly a few hours to ~1 day of runtime versus weeks. For a device whose entire job is to display a near-static FREE/BUSY string, polling a volatile flag every 100 ms is the wrong model.
fix: Make Core2 event-driven like CoreInk: enable automatic light sleep with esp_pm_configure({max_freq_mhz=80,min_freq_mhz=10,light_sleep_enable=true}), capture the loop TaskHandle, and replace delay(100) with ulTaskNotifyTake(pdTRUE, portMAX_DELAY); have the WriteCallback call xTaskNotifyGive(taskHandle) to wake the loop only when a new message arrives. Also call WiFi.mode(WIFI_OFF) and esp_bt_controller_mem_release(ESP_BT_MODE_CLASSIC_BT) at boot. This alone cuts idle current by an order of magnitude.
verification: Flash, leave idle on battery, measure current with a USB/inline power meter (e.g. M5.Power.getBatteryVoltage drop over time, or external uA meter): idle current should drop from tens of mA to low single-digit mA. Confirm a BLE write still updates the LCD within ~1 s.

title: Core2 LCD backlight left at full brightness permanently
problem: M5.begin() powers the Core2 LCD backlight at default (max) brightness and the code never calls M5.Display.setBrightness() nor dims/turns off the panel. The Core2 backlight LED alone draws on the order of 40-80 mA at full brightness — this dominates total power and by itself makes multi-day battery life impossible. The display content is static FREE/BUSY text that does not need a bright always-on backlight.
fix: After M5.Display.setRotation(1), call M5.Display.setBrightness(low value, e.g. 30-60 out of 255). Better: dim or turn the backlight fully off after N seconds of no interaction (M5.Display.setBrightness(0) / M5.Display.sleep()) and wake it briefly on touch/button or on a state change in the WriteCallback. For a presence display, an always-dim or on-demand backlight is appropriate.
verification: Measure battery current with setBrightness(255) vs setBrightness(40): expect ~30-60 mA reduction. Visually confirm text is still legible at the chosen brightness.

title: AgentOrchestrator uses `logger` that is never imported — NameError crashes the API poll loop
problem: service.py references `logger.warning(...)` at line 113 but `logger` is never imported or defined anywhere in the file (no `from bumeet_agent.logging import get_logger`, no `logger = get_logger(__name__)`). The moment the API returns HTTP 401 (expired/rejected agent token — a normal, expected condition per the comment), `_api_poll_loop` raises `NameError: name 'logger' is not defined`. The `try` only catches `(TimeoutError, aiohttp.ClientError)`, so the NameError propagates out of the loop, the fire-and-forget task dies (its exception is never awaited), and calendar/Slack presence updates stop forever with no log and no recovery until process restart. Guaranteed crash on the single most likely error path.
fix: Add the logger at module top: `from bumeet_agent.logging import get_logger` then `logger = get_logger(__name__)`. Grep: `grep -n 'logger' src/bumeet_agent/detection/service.py` should show a definition before first use.
verification: python -c "import bumeet_agent.detection.service as s; assert hasattr(s,'logger')"; add a unit test driving `_api_poll_loop` against a stub returning 401 and assert it logs and keeps running rather than raising NameError.

title: Unauthenticated POST /auth/oauth-login issues a session for ANY email (account takeover)
problem: oauthLogin accepts an unauthenticated body { provider, email, name } and AuthService.oauthLogin (auth.service.ts:56-64) looks up or creates a user by that email and immediately returns a valid 7-day session token. There is no OAuth code exchange, no provider verification, and no proof the caller controls the email. Anyone can POST { email: 'victim@corp.com' } and receive a fully authenticated session for that user — complete account takeover, plus arbitrary account creation. The body isn't even a validated DTO (raw inline type), so whitelist stripping does not apply.
fix: Remove this endpoint entirely, or gate it behind a verified provider token. The real OAuth flow already exists via /auth/<provider>/callback which performs a server-side code exchange — login should only mint a session after that exchange returns a verified email. If a first-party social-login is needed, verify a signed id_token from the provider (validate signature, aud, iss, exp) before calling createSession.
verification: curl -X POST /api/v1/auth/oauth-login -d '{"provider":"google","email":"someone-else@x.com"}' must NOT return a token. Confirm the route is gone (404) or returns 401 without a verified provider assertion.

title: JWT signing/verification falls back to the hardcoded 'fallback-secret' when JWT_SECRET is unset
problem: Both signing (auth.service.ts:48), JwtModule registration (auth.module.ts:17) and verification (jwt.strategy.ts:15) use config.get('JWT_SECRET') || 'fallback-secret'. If JWT_SECRET is missing/misconfigured in any deployment, the app silently boots with a publicly-known secret, letting anyone forge tokens for arbitrary sub/sessionId. The example secret in .env.example ('your-super-secret-jwt-key-change-in-production') is also a known value. There is no fail-fast on a missing secret.
fix: Remove all 'fallback-secret' defaults and fail fast at startup if JWT_SECRET is absent or too short: in main.ts/bootstrap, if (!process.env.JWT_SECRET || process.env.JWT_SECRET.length < 32) throw. Use ConfigModule validationSchema (Joi) to require it.
verification: Boot the app with JWT_SECRET unset; it must refuse to start. Confirm a token signed with 'fallback-secret' is rejected (401) in a properly configured instance.

title: Core2 builds String from c_str(), truncating UTF-8 payload at first NUL and ignoring length
problem: String incoming(val.c_str()) constructs the Arduino String from a C-string, so it stops at the first 0x00 byte and drops the explicit val.size(). The documented payload is 'UTF-8, max 64 bytes' and can legitimately contain the middle-dot separator ' · ' (U+00B7 -> 0xC2 0xB7), which is fine, but any embedded NUL (e.g. a malformed/padded agent write, or a multi-byte sequence the agent zero-pads) silently truncates the message and can cause it to be parsed as a different state. The CoreInk version correctly uses String incoming(val.c_str(), val.size()). This is an inconsistency between the two firmwares for the same wire protocol.
fix: Use the length-aware constructor exactly like CoreInk: String incoming(val.c_str(), val.size()); (or val.data()/val.length()). Keeps binary-safety and matches the agent contract.
verification: Send a BLE write containing the ' · ' separator and a trailing payload; confirm the full source/endTime render on the LCD. Send a payload with an embedded NUL and confirm it is not silently truncated.

title: Core2 writes to NVS flash inside the BLE host callback on every state change
problem: onWrite calls gPrefs.begin()/putString()/end() directly in the NimBLE host-task context for every distinct incoming message. (1) NVS writes are blocking flash operations performed from the BLE callback, which can stall the BLE host and cause connection supervision timeouts. (2) There is no de-dup against the last persisted value (CoreInk tracks gLastPersistedMsg and only writes when it actually changed), so a chatty agent that toggles BUSY·ends 15:30 -> BUSY·ends 15:31 every minute wears the NVS flash. ESP32 NVS has limited erase cycles; sustained per-minute writes can wear the partition over the device's life. (3) Opening/closing the Preferences namespace on every write is wasteful.
fix: Move persistence out of the callback into the loop (as CoreInk does): in onWrite only set gPendingMsg/gNeedsRedraw and notify the task. In the loop, after rendering, persist only if the value differs from a gLastPersistedMsg tracker, and open gPrefs once in setup() with gPrefs.begin("bumeet", false) kept open.
verification: Instrument a counter or log around putString; drive rapid state changes from the agent and confirm NVS is written only on genuine changes and never from the BLE task. Confirm BLE connection stays up during writes.

title: gCurrentMsg / gLastPersistedMsg String shared across BLE task and loop without the mutex
problem: The portMUX critical section only protects gPendingMsg and gNeedsRedraw. But the BLE host task reads gCurrentMsg at line 199 (`if (incoming == gCurrentMsg) return;`) while the main loop concurrently writes gCurrentMsg at line 358 (`gCurrentMsg = toRender;`). Arduino String assignment frees the old buffer and reallocates; reading the String from another core/task while it is being reassigned is a data race that can read a dangling/half-updated pointer and crash or corrupt the heap. isMajorTransition() (line 100-105) also reads gCurrentMsg from the loop, and renderMessage uses it at line 163 — all unprotected. The same applies to gLastPersistedMsg (loop-only, OK) but gCurrentMsg is genuinely concurrent.
fix: Either (a) move the `incoming == gCurrentMsg` early-out out of the callback and instead compare against gPendingMsg under the existing critical section, or (b) protect every read/write of gCurrentMsg with gMsgMux, or (c) keep a separate atomic snapshot string updated only under the mutex for the callback to compare against. Simplest: in onWrite, drop the gCurrentMsg compare and just store gPendingMsg under the mux; let the loop dedupe against gCurrentMsg (loop-local, single-threaded there).
verification: Stress test: have the agent hammer alternating distinct messages at high rate while the loop renders; run with CONFIG_SPIRAM/heap poisoning or -fsanitize-like ESP heap debugging (heap_caps_check_integrity) and confirm no corruption over thousands of transitions.

title: Camera detection forks up to two `ioreg` subprocesses every poll (~2s) — dominant battery/CPU drain
problem: `_poll_camera()` runs `subprocess.run(['ioreg', ...])` for AppleH13CamIn, and when that misses (the common idle case) runs a SECOND `subprocess.run(['ioreg', ...])` for IOVideoDeviceStream, on every snapshot. With default `poll_interval_seconds=2.0` (config.py:38) that is ~1-2 process fork+exec + full IORegistry walks every 2s whenever the camera is NOT in use (steady state), i.e. ~1,800+ ioreg spawns/hour. ioreg walks the IO registry and is far heavier than a syscall; repeated fork/exec on macOS prevents low-power idle states and is a well-known battery killer for menu-bar agents. The CoreAudio mic check is cheap by comparison; the camera path dominates power draw.
fix: (1) Replace ioreg subprocess with an in-process CoreMediaIO/IOKit ctypes check like the audio path. (2) Decouple camera cadence from mic cadence — poll the camera every 10-15s (join/leave is not latency-critical) and run the IOVideoDeviceStream fallback once at startup to pick the platform path, not every tick. Going 2s→15s cuts spawns ~7.5x.
verification: Run idle 60s and count spawns: `sudo dtrace -n 'proc:::exec-success/execname=="ioreg"/{@=count()}'` — should drop from ~30/min to a few/min. Compare powermetrics energy impact before/after.

title: Persistent BLE connection loop wakes every 1s forever, preventing CPU idle
problem: `_connection_loop` ends every iteration with `await asyncio.sleep(1)` (line 119) and runs for the entire agent lifetime. Even when connected and idle (keepalive only every 20s, reconnect 5s), the loop wakes the event loop once per second to re-check `is_connected` and a timestamp. This is a 1Hz wakeup that prevents the process and asyncio timer from coalescing into longer sleeps, hurting battery on an otherwise-idle laptop. The 1s granularity is far finer than any time-based action it performs.
fix: Make the loop sleep until the next scheduled action: compute `_KEEPALIVE_INTERVAL_S - (now - _last_write_time)` and `await asyncio.wait_for(event.wait(), timeout=that_delay)` so it sleeps ~20s when idle and wakes immediately on a real write or disconnect. Use bleak's `disconnected_callback` to trigger reconnect instead of 1Hz polling of `is_connected`.
verification: Add a test asserting at most 1 wake per keepalive interval when connected+idle. On hardware, powermetrics should show fewer wakeups/sec for the agent process.

title: API poll loop hammers a known-dead endpoint every 5s after 401 with no backoff
problem: On HTTP 401 the loop logs and does `await asyncio.sleep(interval)` + `continue`, re-issuing the same authenticated GET to `/agent/live-status` every `poll_interval_seconds` (default 5.0, config.py:46) forever. Once the agent token is rejected the endpoint keeps returning 401, so this is an infinite stream of redundant network calls every 5s (720/hour) that can never succeed — wasting radio/battery and adding server load with no exponential backoff and no circuit-breaker. The only documented recovery is manual re-pairing.
fix: On 401, back off exponentially (from `interval` up to several minutes) or stop polling and surface a re-pair prompt, resuming only after the token refreshes. Honor any server `Retry-After`. Guard with a max-failure counter that widens the sleep.
verification: Unit-test `_api_poll_loop` with a stub returning 401 repeatedly; assert the inter-call sleep grows (backoff) rather than staying at `interval`.

title: Keepalive failure calls disconnect() and continues without sleeping — tight reconnect spin on a flapping link
problem: In the keepalive branch, on write failure it calls `await self.disconnect()` then `continue` (lines 116-117) with NO sleep before looping. The next iteration sees `not is_connected` and immediately retries `connect()`. When the link is flapping (connect succeeds but write fails), this churns connect→write-fail→disconnect→connect rapidly because the connected-branch failure path has no delay, only the connect-failure path sleeps `_RECONNECT_INTERVAL_S`. On battery this is a high-power tight loop of BLE connect/disconnect.
fix: After `disconnect()` in the keepalive failure branch, add `await asyncio.sleep(_RECONNECT_INTERVAL_S)` before `continue`, mirroring the connect-failure path. Route all failure exits through one backoff sleep so no path re-enters connect without delay.
verification: Test with a fake client whose `write_gatt_char` always raises after a successful connect; assert reconnect attempts are spaced ≥ `_RECONNECT_INTERVAL_S` and the loop does not spin.

title: Reconnect can re-send a never-delivered/stale `_last_payload`; two separate copies of last state drift
problem: BleClient initializes `self._last_payload = b'FREE'` (line 53) and updates it inside `write_now` at line 132 BEFORE confirming delivery — then waits for `_connected_event` and may return early on timeout (line 137) having recorded a payload that was never transmitted. On reconnect, `_connection_loop` re-sends `_last_payload` (lines 89-93) to resync the e-ink, so it can resync to a state the firmware never received. Separately, AgentOrchestrator keeps its OWN `_last_payload` (service.py:72) used by the heartbeat, creating two sources of truth that can drift.
fix: Make BleClient the single owner: update `_last_payload` only AFTER `send_payload` returns successfully in `write_now`. Remove the orchestrator's parallel `_last_payload` and have the heartbeat call a `ble_client.resend_last()` so there is exactly one authoritative payload.
verification: Test: call write_now while disconnected so it times out, then trigger reconnect; assert the un-delivered payload is not pushed and orchestrator/BleClient agree on the last confirmed payload.

title: Permanent agent API token stored in plaintext JSON with default permissions, not the OS keychain
problem: `SettingsStore.save` writes settings — including `api.token`, the permanent `x-agent-key` bearer credential saved after pairing (app.py:131) — to `~/.config/bumeet-agent/config.json` (config.py:81-82) as plaintext JSON with umask-default permissions (typically 0644). A long-lived credential that impersonates the agent to the cloud API is recoverable by any local process/user and ends up in Time Machine/backups in cleartext. The token is never rotated.
fix: Store the token in macOS Keychain / Windows Credential Manager via `keyring`, keeping only non-secret settings in JSON. If JSON is unavoidable, `mkdir(mode=0o700)` the parent and `os.chmod(path, 0o600)` after write, write atomically (tmpfile + os.replace), and mark the field `pydantic.SecretStr`.
verification: After pairing, `ls -l ~/.config/bumeet-agent/config.json` shows 0600 (or token absent from JSON if moved to keyring); confirm `keyring.get_password` returns it.

title: Windows hardware detection raises NotImplementedError — agent runs with detection silently dead on Windows
problem: `WindowsHardwareDetector.start` raises `NotImplementedError` (windows.py:12). In `run()` the detector is built (app.py:201) and scheduled via bare `asyncio.create_task(detector.start(...))` (app.py:221). On Windows this task raises immediately; it is only awaited in the shutdown `finally` with `wait_for(..., timeout=3.0)` catching only TimeoutError/CancelledError (app.py:227-229), so the exception surfaces as an unretrieved-task warning and the agent runs with NO detection while appearing 'up'. The product claims Windows support but the core mic/camera feature silently never works.
fix: Implement the Windows detector (HKCU\\...\\CapabilityAccessManager\\ConsentStore\\{microphone,webcam} 'LastUsedTimeStop'==0 means in use, or WinRT AppCapability), OR fail fast at startup with a clear message and non-zero exit instead of scheduling a task that throws. At minimum, await the first detection result / attach a done-callback that logs and triggers shutdown.
verification: Run on Windows: the agent should detect mic/cam usage or exit with a clear 'not supported' error and non-zero code — not silently run with detection dead.

title: logout() never deletes the session (passes userId where sessionId is expected)
problem: The logout endpoint calls this.auth.logout(req.user.id). req.user is the User object returned by JwtStrategy.validate (it returns session.user), so req.user.id is the USER id, not the session id. AuthService.logout (auth.service.ts:66-69) runs prisma.session.deleteMany({ where: { id: sessionId } }) using that user id as the session primary key, which matches zero rows. Logout silently no-ops: the session row survives, and because the JWT itself remains valid for 7 days and the strategy only checks session.expiresAt, the 'logged out' token keeps working. There is no way to revoke a session via logout, defeating the entire server-side session model.
fix: Carry the sessionId through to the request user and delete by it. In jwt.strategy.ts validate(), return { ...session.user, sessionId: session.id } (or attach payload.sessionId). Then in the controller call this.auth.logout(req.user.sessionId), and keep deleteMany({ where: { id: sessionId } }). Alternatively change logout signature to accept userId and deleteMany({ where: { userId } }) if 'log out everywhere' is intended — but the single-session intent requires the sessionId.
verification: Login, capture token, call POST /api/v1/auth/logout, then call GET /api/v1/auth/me with the same token; it must now return 401. Also assert the Session row is gone: SELECT count(*) FROM "Session" WHERE "userId"=... drops by 1.

title: Public GET /auth/demo-login hands out a real session with hardcoded seeded credentials
problem: demoLogin() is unauthenticated and logs in as demo@bumeet.io / Demo1234! — credentials that are committed in prisma/seed.ts (line 9, 122). In any environment seeded with this user, an attacker hits GET /api/v1/auth/demo-login and gets a valid 7-day token, then can read/modify that account's integrations, calendar, OAuth-linked data, and BLE/device config. A GET endpoint with side effects (creates a Session row) is also CSRF-prone and crawlable.
fix: Guard demo-login behind an explicit env flag (e.g. if (process.env.ENABLE_DEMO_LOGIN !== 'true') throw new NotFoundException()) and never enable it in production. Do not seed the demo user in production, and rotate/disable the well-known password. Prefer making it POST.
verification: In production config, GET /api/v1/auth/demo-login returns 404/403. With the flag unset, no Session row is created.

title: OAuth state is just base64(userId) — no CSRF token, no PKCE, attacker controls account binding
problem: Every provider builds state as Buffer.from(userId).toString('base64') (google-calendar.service.ts:42, microsoft:37, teams:30, slack:40, zoom:27, webex:29) and the callback decodes it back to userId and trusts it (e.g. google-calendar.service.ts:47, and auth.controller.ts passes state straight through). state is not random, not signed, and not tied to the user's session, so it provides zero CSRF protection: an attacker can craft a consent URL with state=base64(attackerUserId) and trick a victim into completing it, binding the victim's Google/Microsoft/Slack account tokens to the ATTACKER's BUMEET account (or vice-versa, a login-CSRF). userId is also leaked in the URL/logs. None of the authorization-code flows use PKCE (code_challenge), and the Google client even has a confidential client secret, so a public-client downgrade is possible.
fix: Generate a cryptographically random state per request, store it server-side (Redis or the Session row) bound to the initiating user's session, and verify-then-consume it in handleCallback before trusting any userId. Derive userId from that server-side record, not from the inbound state. Add PKCE: generate a code_verifier, send code_challenge in getAuthUrl, and pass code_verifier in exchangeCode for every provider.
verification: Replaying a callback with a forged/old state must fail. Confirm state values are random per-request and single-use (a second callback with the same state is rejected). Confirm token requests include code_verifier.

title: OAuth access/refresh tokens and Apple app-specific passwords stored in plaintext
problem: IntegrationAccount.accessToken/refreshToken (schema.prisma:52-53) are plain String columns and are written verbatim by every provider (e.g. google-calendar.service.ts:66-67, microsoft:59, slack:63, zoom:47, webex:49). Apple Calendar stores the user's App-Specific Password directly in accessToken and the principal URL in refreshToken (apple-calendar.service.ts:41-42). These are long-lived, broadly-scoped credentials (Calendars.Read, Presence.Read, Slack channels:history/im:history, full iCloud CalDAV). Any DB read, backup leak, or SQL-injection turns into full compromise of every connected user's Google/Microsoft/Slack/Zoom/Webex/iCloud account. No encryption-at-rest in the app layer.
fix: Encrypt tokens at rest with an envelope/AEAD scheme (e.g. AES-256-GCM via Node crypto, key from a KMS/Key Vault, not from .env). Add encrypt()/decrypt() helpers and apply them on every write/read of accessToken/refreshToken. At minimum, segregate the encryption key from the database. Treat Apple app passwords with the same protection.
verification: SELECT "accessToken" FROM "IntegrationAccount" returns ciphertext, not a usable token. App can still call provider APIs after decrypt.

title: Rate limiting is configured but never enforced — ThrottlerGuard not registered as APP_GUARD
problem: ThrottlerModule.forRoot([{ ttl: 60000, limit: 100 }]) is imported (app.module.ts:17) but ThrottlerGuard is never provided as an APP_GUARD and no @UseGuards(ThrottlerGuard)/@Throttle is applied anywhere (grep for ThrottlerGuard/APP_GUARD/@Throttle returns nothing). In NestJS, ThrottlerModule alone does nothing without the guard, so there is effectively NO rate limiting. POST /auth/login (argon2 verify) and /auth/register are wide open to credential-stuffing/brute force; the agent pairing endpoints (/agent/pair/status, /agent/pair/approve) and the public OAuth-login endpoint can be hammered freely.
fix: Register the guard globally in app.module.ts providers: { provide: APP_GUARD, useClass: ThrottlerGuard }. Add a stricter @Throttle limit specifically on auth and pairing routes. Ensure a trust-proxy/keyGenerator is set so per-IP limits work behind Azure/Cloudflare (otherwise all traffic shares one proxy IP).
verification: Fire 200 rapid POST /api/v1/auth/login requests from one IP; responses must start returning 429 after the configured limit.

title: No indexes on userId / integrationId foreign keys — hot queries do sequential scans
problem: The schema defines only PKs and unique constraints; there are no @@index declarations (confirmed: grep '@@index' returns nothing, and migrations create only the unique/PK indexes). The two hottest queries scan unindexed columns: getBusyStatus (integrations.service.ts:305-315) filters CalendarEvent by userId + allDay + startAt + endAt + status, and getEvents (calendar.service.ts:22-26) filters by userId+startAt — neither CalendarEvent.userId nor (userId, startAt) is indexed. CalendarEvent.integrationId (used by deleteMany on every sync, e.g. google-calendar.service.ts:192) is unindexed. MessageToDisplay.userId (messages.service.ts:9) and Session.userId (users.service.ts:45) are unindexed. getBusyStatus runs on the agent poll loop (every 5s per device) AND inside the 60s server-wide auto-sync getLiveStatus path, so these seq scans hit constantly and will not scale past a few thousand events.
fix: Add to schema.prisma: on CalendarEvent @@index([userId, startAt]) and @@index([integrationId]); on MessageToDisplay @@index([userId, createdAt]); on Session @@index([userId]); on IntegrationAccount @@index([userId]). Generate a migration and apply.
verification: EXPLAIN ANALYZE the getBusyStatus query before/after; confirm it uses an Index Scan on the new (userId, startAt) index instead of Seq Scan.

title: Calendar auto-sync runs every 60s (comment says 15 min) — N external API calls/min per integration, no de-dup or backoff
problem: onModuleInit sets setInterval(() => this.syncAllCalendars(), 60_000) while the section comment claims 'every 15 min' (integrations.service.ts:32-34). Every 60s it loads ALL active google/microsoft/zoom/webex integrations across ALL users and calls syncEvents on each (lines 38-50). Each syncEvents does full paginated pulls (Google events.list looping all pages, MS calendarView, Zoom/Webex meetings) plus per-event upserts and a deleteMany — so this is a fixed, ever-growing per-minute load on both the external APIs (rate-limit/quota burn, e.g. Google Calendar API, Zoom) and the DB. There is no jitter, no per-integration min-interval, no backoff on failure, and a long-running sync can overlap the next tick (no in-flight guard). If the process is multi-instance, every instance runs the full loop, multiplying the load.
fix: Restore a sane cadence (e.g. 5-15 min) and add an in-flight guard so a tick is skipped if the previous run hasn't finished. Track per-integration lastSyncAt and skip ones synced recently. Move scheduling to @nestjs/schedule (@Cron) with a distributed lock (Redis — already a dependency) so only one instance runs it. Use webhooks/push (Google watch, MS subscriptions) instead of polling where possible. Fix the misleading comment.
verification: Log the per-tick integration count and external API call count; confirm calls/min drop to the intended cadence and two app instances don't both run the loop.

title: getLiveStatus fans out a live HTTP call to every presence provider on every agent poll (every 5s), no caching
problem: getLiveStatus (called by the agent /agent/live-status and /integrations/live-status) issues a fresh remote presence fetch for every Slack/Teams/Microsoft/Zoom/Webex integration the user has (integrations.service.ts:77-91), each a separate network round-trip, plus a token-refresh-on-expiry write inside several of them. The agent config tells devices to poll every 5s (agent.controller.ts:43 pollInterval: 5). So per device this is N external presence API calls every 5 seconds (720 calls/hour/provider), which will trip Slack/Graph/Zoom rate limits and adds 5x token-refresh DB writes. ioredis is a declared dependency but no caching layer exists anywhere.
fix: Cache presence per integration in Redis with a short TTL (e.g. 15-30s) keyed by integrationId, and serve live-status from cache; refresh out-of-band. Decouple presence polling cadence from the device poll. Coalesce concurrent identical requests. Raise pollInterval or switch the device to long-poll/SSE/WebSocket so the server pushes changes instead of being polled.
verification: Hit /agent/live-status 12 times in 60s and assert the number of outbound provider HTTP calls is bounded by the cache TTL, not 12*N.

title: Public /api/debug-env endpoint leaks environment configuration
problem: An unauthenticated GET /api/debug-env returns which auth/OAuth env vars are SET vs MISSING and echoes NEXTAUTH_URL, AUTH_URL, NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL and NODE_ENV verbatim. This is a reconnaissance gift to an attacker: it reveals the backend API origin, which providers are configured, whether AUTH_SECRET is set, and the deployment URL — all without any credential. It will ship to production because nothing gates it.
fix: Delete the route entirely, or gate it behind a server-only check that 404s in production, e.g. `if (process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production') return new NextResponse(null, { status: 404 });` and additionally require an admin session. Preferred: remove the file `src/app/api/debug-env/route.ts`.
verification: After removal/guard, `curl -i https://app.bumeet.es/api/debug-env` returns 404 in production. Run `npm run build` to confirm no references remain.
locationNote: REAL issue. The code exists exactly as described. title: Backend API JWT (apiToken) is exposed to client-side JavaScript and rendered into the DOM
problem: The NextAuth session() callback copies the backend bearer token onto the session object, so it is returned by the client-readable /api/auth/session endpoint and consumed via useSession() everywhere (e.g. messages/integrations/account pages). On the Device page it is even interpolated directly into install command strings rendered as visible text (device/page.tsx:58-68) and into a clipboard copy. Any XSS, malicious browser extension, or shoulder-surf exposes a long-lived API credential. The httpOnly protection of the NextAuth cookie is bypassed by deliberately surfacing the raw token to JS.
fix: Keep the backend token server-side only: do not attach it to the session in the session() callback. Instead, proxy API calls through Next.js Route Handlers / server actions that read the token from the encrypted JWT (via `auth()`) and forward it, so the browser never holds the raw bearer. For the Device install command, mint a short-lived, single-use pairing token from the backend rather than embedding the permanent apiToken in a curl string shown on screen.
verification: Run `await fetch('/api/auth/session').then(r=>r.json())` in the browser console and confirm no apiToken/bearer is present; confirm dashboard pages still load data through the new server proxy.

Line numbers 89-92 are exactly correct — the session() callback at line 89-92 does `(session as any).apiToken = token.apiToken; return session;`, surfacing the backend bearer token into the client-readable session.

- 6 client components read `(session as any)?.apiToken` via useSession() (page.tsx:40, messages/page.tsx:358, status/page.tsx:19, integrations/page.tsx:48, device/page.tsx:56, account/page.tsx:18). useSession() fetches the token through the client-readable /api/auth/session endpoint, so the raw bearer is held in browser JS.

This bypasses the httpOnly protection of the NextAuth cookie by deliberately exposing the raw token to JS. Not a false positive, not already handled.

Proposed fix is safe and correct in direction (keep token server-side; proxy API calls through Route Handlers/server actions that read the token via auth() from the encrypted JWT; mint short-lived single-use pairing tokens for device install instead of embedding the 7d token in curl strings). It is a substantial multi-file refactor, not a one-liner. Note: the repo already has a pairing-code mechanism (platform/apps/api/src/pairing/pairing.controller.ts returns expiresInSeconds: 300, and device/page.tsx already supports a ?pair=CODE approve flow), so the short-lived-pairing-token half of the fix is partially backed by existing infrastructure and is the natural path for the device install command.

title: NextAuth falls back to a hardcoded 'fallback-secret'
problem: `secret: process.env.NEXTAUTH_SECRET || 'fallback-secret'` means that if NEXTAUTH_SECRET (and AUTH_SECRET) are ever unset in an environment, sessions are signed/encrypted with a publicly-known constant string committed to the repo. An attacker who knows this value can forge valid session JWTs and impersonate any user. A silent fallback also masks misconfiguration instead of failing fast.
fix: Remove the fallback and fail loudly: `secret: process.env.AUTH_SECRET ?? process.env.NEXTAUTH_SECRET` and let NextAuth throw if undefined, or add `if (!process.env.AUTH_SECRET && !process.env.NEXTAUTH_SECRET) throw new Error('AUTH_SECRET is required')` at module load.
verification: Build with the secret unset and confirm startup throws; grep the bundle for 'fallback-secret' to confirm it is gone: `grep -rn fallback-secret src .next`.

title: Postgres 'auto-pause' is misdiagnosed; SELECT 1 keepalive cannot prevent an explicit az stop
problem: Commit ebdde777 claims Azure PostgreSQL Flexible Server Burstable (B1ms) 'auto-pauses after inactivity' and adds a 20-min `SELECT 1` keepalive in PrismaService. This is incorrect: Azure PostgreSQL Flexible Server has NO idle auto-pause — it only stops when explicitly told to. The real cause of P1001 'server paused' is the scheduled workflow dev-resources-stop.yml which runs `az postgres flexible-server stop` every day at 19:00 UTC (line 37-50). A `SELECT 1` query cannot override an administrative stop, so the keepalive solves a non-existent failure mode while masking the actual one. Worse, dev App Service runs with always_on=false (envs/dev/main.tf:8), so the App Service worker unloads after ~20 min idle and the setInterval timer stops firing — the keepalive does not even run when it would supposedly be needed. Net effect: dead code that creates a false sense of safety and confuses future operators about why the DB is unreachable each morning.
fix: Remove the keepalive from PrismaService entirely. Document that the dev DB is intentionally stopped nightly by dev-resources-stop.yml and brought back via dev-resources-start.yml. If you genuinely need the dev DB warm during working hours, add a scheduled `dev-resources-start` cron (e.g. weekdays 07:00 UTC) instead of an in-process timer. For prod, do not stop the server at all (it isn't in the stop workflow, which is correct). If P1001 on cold start is the concern, add Prisma connection retry with backoff at bootstrap rather than a periodic ping.
verification: az postgres flexible-server show -n psql-bumeet-dev -g rg-bumeet-dev --query state -o tsv at 03:00 local should be 'Stopped'; confirm the morning P1001 disappears only after adding a scheduled start, not after the keepalive. Grep confirms keepalive: git show ebdde777.

title: ACR admin user enabled — long-lived shared registry credentials instead of managed identity
problem: container_registry/main.tf:7 sets `admin_enabled = true`. The ACR admin account is a single shared username/password with full push/pull rights that cannot be scoped, rotated per-consumer, or audited per-identity. It was enabled (commit 3cd9caee) purely so `az acr login` and App Service image pull would work. App Service already has a SystemAssigned managed identity (app_service/main.tf:18-20) that should pull images via an AcrPull role assignment; CI authenticates via azure/login SP and can push with that identity using `az acr login`. Admin creds are a standing credential-theft target and are typically what leaks into pipeline logs or app settings.
fix: Set admin_enabled = false. Add `resource azurerm_role_assignment acr_pull { scope = module.container_registry.id; role_definition_name = "AcrPull"; principal_id = module.app_service.principal_id }` and configure the web app to pull with managed identity (azurerm_linux_web_app site_config { container_registry_use_managed_identity = true } plus DOCKER_REGISTRY_SERVER_URL). Grant the CI service principal AcrPush on the registry. Remove any DOCKER_REGISTRY_SERVER_PASSWORD app settings.
verification: terraform plan shows admin_enabled false and a new AcrPull role_assignment; `az acr credential show -n acrbumeetdev` should fail with admin disabled; redeploy via api-deploy.yml and confirm the App Service still pulls the image.

title: PostgreSQL exposed to all Azure datacenters with no VNet/private endpoint
problem: The only firewall rule is `allow-azure-services` (0.0.0.0/0.0.0.0), which permits any resource in ANY Azure customer's subscription to reach the DB at the network layer — it is not limited to your tenant. Combined with public_network_access enabled by default (no `public_network_access_enabled = false` and no `delegated_subnet_id` set), the Postgres server has a public endpoint reachable from the entire Azure backbone, defended only by the admin password. There is no VNet integration, no private endpoint, and no NSG anywhere in the codebase (grep for private_endpoint/subnet/virtual_network returns nothing).
fix: Preferred: deploy the Flexible Server with private access — create a VNet + delegated subnet, set `delegated_subnet_id` and `private_dns_zone_id`, set `public_network_access_enabled = false`, and VNet-integrate the App Service so it reaches the DB privately. Remove the 0.0.0.0 rule. If staying public short-term, at minimum scope firewall rules to the App Service outbound IPs (azurerm_linux_web_app.possible_outbound_ip_address_list) rather than all-Azure.
verification: az postgres flexible-server show --query network shows publicNetworkAccess=Disabled and a delegatedSubnetResourceId; `psql` from an unrelated public host times out; App Service health check /api/v1/health still returns 200.

title: DB password and Redis key stored in plaintext in Terraform state; state SA lacks hardening
problem: DATABASE-URL (main.tf:152) embeds pg_admin_login and pg_admin_password, and REDIS-URL (main.tf:161) embeds the Redis primary_access_key. All of these land in the Terraform state file in clear text. The state lives in storage account stbumeetterraform (bootstrap/main.tf:43), which has no `allow_blob_public_access = false`, no `shared_access_key_enabled = false`, no `public_network_access_enabled`/network_rules restriction, and no infrastructure encryption or CMK. Anyone with the storage account key or list access to the tfstate container can read every secret. The connection-string outputs (outputs.tf:46-56) and module sensitive outputs are also persisted in state.
fix: Harden the state SA in bootstrap: add allow_nested_items_to_be_public=false, shared_access_key_enabled=false (use Azure AD auth for the backend with use_azuread_auth=true), public_network_access via network_rules default_action=Deny with the CI runner range/private endpoint, infrastructure_encryption_enabled=true. Restrict access to the tfstate container with RBAC (Storage Blob Data Contributor) only for the CI SP. Rotate the pg admin password and Redis key after locking down. Long-term, generate DB creds outside TF (e.g. Key Vault-generated) so they never enter state, or use managed identity for Postgres (Entra admin) to eliminate the password.
verification: az storage account show -n stbumeetterraform --query 'allowBlobPublicAccess,allowSharedKeyAccess,publicNetworkAccess'; terraform state pull | grep -c admin_password should be reviewed and access locked; confirm backend still initializes with use_azuread_auth.

title: Key Vault purge protection disabled in all environments including prod
problem: key_vault/main.tf:10 hardcodes `purge_protection_enabled = false` for every environment with a comment 'Set to true in prod after initial stable apply'. With purge protection off, a deleted or purged vault (accidental `terraform destroy`, a malicious actor with Purge permission, or a compromised CI SP — which holds Purge per main.tf:17) is permanently and immediately destroyable, taking DATABASE-URL and REDIS-URL with it and breaking the running App Service that resolves @Microsoft.KeyVault references at runtime. soft_delete_retention is only 7 days (variables.tf:105) and the CI SP secret_permissions include Delete and Purge, so a bad apply can wipe secrets irrecoverably.
fix: Set purge_protection_enabled = true for prod (drive it from a variable, e.g. var.env == "prod"). Remove Purge from the CI service principal's secret_permissions (key_vault/main.tf:17) — CI should not be able to purge. Increase soft_delete_retention_days for prod to 30+. Note purge protection cannot be disabled once enabled, which is the intended safety property.
verification: terraform plan for prod shows purge_protection_enabled true; az keyvault show -n kv-bumeet-prod --query properties.enablePurgeProtection returns true; attempting az keyvault purge is rejected.

title: No monitoring, Application Insights, Log Analytics, or alerts anywhere in the stack

There is a health_check_path configured (app_service/main.tf:30) but no metric alert on health-check failures, no Application Insights for the NestJS API, no Log Analytics workspace, no diagnostic settings on Postgres/Redis/App Service/Key Vault, and no action group to notify anyone. A prod outage (DB down, 5xx spike, Redis eviction, cert expiry, App Service restart loop) is invisible until a user reports it. The prod env even tags itself sla=99.9 (envs/prod/main.tf:23) with zero observability to back that claim.

Add azurerm_monitor_diagnostic_setting for App Service, Postgres, Redis, Key Vault -> the workspace. Add azurerm_monitor_metric_alert for HTTP 5xx, HealthCheckStatus, Postgres CPU/storage/connection-failures, Redis evicted-keys/used-memory, and an azurerm_monitor_action_group emailing the team. Add a cert-expiry alert for the custom domains.

title: Prod Postgres, App Service plan, and Redis are all single-instance with no zone redundancy (SPOF) despite 99.9 SLA tag
problem: Prod is tagged sla=99.9 (envs/prod/main.tf:23) but every tier is a single point of failure: (1) Postgres has no high_availability block, so it is a single node with no zone-redundant or same-zone standby; an AZ or node failure means a full outage and a restore-from-backup RTO measured in tens of minutes. (2) The App Service plan P1v3 (envs/prod/main.tf:7) is provisioned but there is no zone_balancing_enabled and no worker_count > 1 (app_service/main.tf:1-8 has no capacity), so a single instance handles all traffic with no rolling-restart headroom. (3) Redis Standard C1 (envs/prod/main.tf:14-16) is a single shard; while Standard has a replica, there is no clustering for scale. A single-AZ outage takes prod fully down. Single-instance App Service / non-HA Postgres are NOT covered by a 99.9% composite SLA.
fix: For prod Postgres add `high_availability { mode = "ZoneRedundant" }` (requires a GP/MO tier, which prod already uses: GP_Standard_D2s_v3). For App Service set zone_balancing_enabled=true and worker_count>=2 (or autoscale rules) on the plan. Re-evaluate the sla tag against the actual composite SLA. Drive these from a per-env variable so dev stays single-instance for cost.
verification: terraform plan prod shows high_availability ZoneRedundant on the server and worker_count>=2 / zone_balancing_enabled on the plan; az postgres flexible-server show --query highAvailability.state returns Healthy.

title: App Service is Terraformed as a Node.js code app but deployed as a Docker container — config drift and broken settings
problem: The stack deploys a Docker image via ACR (api-deploy.yml:42-56 build/push + azure/webapps-deploy with images:), but the App Service module configures a Node code runtime: site_config.application_stack { node_version } (main.tf:26-28), plus app_settings SCM_DO_BUILD_DURING_DEPLOYMENT=true and WEBSITE_NODE_DEFAULT_VERSION=~20 (main.tf:36-37). These are mutually exclusive: a container app must use application_stack { docker_image_name / docker_registry_url } (or linux_fx_version DOCKER|...), and SCM_DO_BUILD/Oryx build settings are meaningless and can break container boot. Every `azure/webapps-deploy` sets the container image out-of-band, so the next `terraform apply` will try to revert the app to the Node stack — guaranteed drift between CI deploys and TF, and a real risk that an apply clobbers the running container config. The node_version variable (api_node_version, variables.tf:30-34) is dead.
fix: Switch the module to a container app: in site_config use application_stack { docker_image_name = "${acr}/bumeet-api:<tag>", docker_registry_url = "https://${acr_login_server}" } and add container_registry_use_managed_identity=true. Remove SCM_DO_BUILD_DURING_DEPLOYMENT and WEBSITE_NODE_DEFAULT_VERSION. Keep WEBSITES_PORT=8080. Add lifecycle { ignore_changes = [site_config[0].application_stack[0].docker_image_name] } so CI image bumps don't drift TF, or feed the tag in as a variable. Remove the unused api_node_version variable.
verification: terraform apply after a CI deploy produces no diff on the web app image; az webapp config show shows linuxFxVersion DOCKER|...; the API responds on /api/v1/health.

title: API deploy hardcodes the dev ACR and dev App Service for main pushes — prod API never gets deployed
problem: api-deploy.yml runs on push to main and hardcodes ACR_REGISTRY=acrbumeetdev.azurecr.io, APP_NAME=app-bumeet-dev-api (lines 18-20). Terraform provisions a separate prod registry acrbumeetprod and a prod app app-bumeet-prod-api (root main.tf:97,125 with env=prod). There is no prod API deploy job anywhere — so every merge to main pushes the image only to the dev registry and deploys only to the dev App Service. The production API is either never updated by CI or must be deployed manually, defeating the dev->prod gating that terraform-apply.yml carefully sets up. This is a release-management correctness defect.
fix: Parameterize registry/app per environment and add a prod deploy job that needs the dev job and targets a GitHub `prod` environment with manual approval (mirroring terraform-apply.yml). Pull ACR_REGISTRY/APP_NAME from environment-scoped variables. Tag images immutably by SHA (already done) and promote the same digest dev->prod rather than rebuilding.

title: terraform apply runs -auto-approve on push to main with no saved plan and no lock-timeout
problem: apply-dev and apply-prod run `terraform apply -auto-approve` directly (lines 43-46, 68-71), re-planning at apply time rather than applying the exact plan that was reviewed in the PR (terraform-plan.yml produces tfplan but it is never persisted/passed to apply). This means what merges is not necessarily what applies — any drift or provider/data-source change between plan and apply is auto-approved with no human gate on dev, and on prod the GitHub environment approval gates an apply whose plan no one has seen. There is also no explicit state-lock handling or -lock-timeout, so a stuck lease blocks deploys.
fix: Persist the reviewed plan: in PR plan, upload tfplan as an artifact (or re-plan in apply and post it, blocking on approval), then `terraform apply -lock-timeout=5m tfplan`. Keep -auto-approve only when applying a pre-approved plan file. Ensure the prod environment approval reviewer sees the plan output before approving.
verification: Apply logs show 'Applying plan from tfplan' with no fresh plan diff; a forced drift between plan and apply causes the job to fail rather than silently apply.

title: Long-lived ARM_CLIENT_SECRET / AZURE_CREDENTIALS used instead of GitHub OIDC federation
problem: Terraform plan/apply auth via ARM_CLIENT_SECRET (terraform-apply.yml:19, terraform-plan.yml:17) and the deploy/start/stop workflows via the full AZURE_CREDENTIALS JSON blob (api-deploy.yml:33, dev-resources-start.yml:24, dev-resources-stop.yml:27). These are long-lived client secrets that must be rotated manually, can leak via logs/forks, and grant standing access. GitHub Actions supports OIDC federated credentials with Azure (azure/login with client-id/tenant-id/subscription-id + id-token: write permission), eliminating stored secrets entirely.

Switch azure/login to OIDC (client-id/tenant-id/subscription-id + permissions: id-token: write) and Terraform to use_oidc=true / ARM_USE_OIDC=true. Delete ARM_CLIENT_SECRET and the AZURE_CREDENTIALS JSON secret.
